notes.body: Terraform reasons about three things: your configuration (.tf files, what you want), the state file (terraform.tfstate, what Terraform last believed existed), and the real cloud (what actually exists). Every plan is a three-way comparison. When you run terraform apply, Terraform saves a JSON snapshot of every resource it created — its provider ID, attributes, and dependencies — into terraform.tfstate. On the next run, it refreshes: it re-reads each real object and compares it against both the state and the config. Worked example: you create azurerm_resource_group.main in config, apply, and the state records its Azure ID. You then rename the resource block label from main to primary in the .tf file without changing anything else. terraform plan proposes to destroy the old object and create a new one — because the state maps labels to IDs, and the new label has no mapping. The fix is terraform state mv azurerm_resource_group.main azurerm_resource_group.primary, which renames the mapping with zero cloud changes. Key interview line: the state file is the map; the config is the destination; never confuse the two.
notes.title: State is Terraform's memory: config, state, reality
Remote backends: shared, locked, durable state

notes.body: State-writing operations — apply, import, state mv — acquire the backend lock first. If engineer A is mid-apply and engineer B runs terraform apply, B's run stops immediately with an error naming the lock holder, and makes zero changes. The lock releases when A's run finishes, even if it fails partway. Worked example of the failure mode locking prevents: without locking, A and B both read state at version 10. A creates a VM and writes version 11. B, still holding the version-10 snapshot, creates a disk and writes version 11 too — overwriting A's VM record. The VM now exists in Azure but in no state file: orphaned, untracked, billed forever. If a run crashes and leaves a stale lock, you confirm no apply is running (check CI logs, ask the team), then run terraform force-unlock <lock-id> — a deliberate manual step, never scripted. Interview line: locking turns a silent corruption into a loud, safe error; force-unlock is a human decision, not an automation step.
notes.title: State locking: what happens when two applies collide

notes.body:
Drift is any change made outside Terraform — a teammate resizing a VM in the portal, an autoscaler swapping a SKU, a disk added by hand. During refresh (the default first phase of plan and apply), Terraform re-reads each managed object; anything that differs from state is drift. Worked example: your config sets azurerm_virtual_machine.app vm_size = "Standard_D2s_v3". Someone changes it to Standard_D4s_v3 in the Azure portal. Next terraform plan shows:

  ~ vm_size = "Standard_D2s_v3" -> "Standard_D4s_v3"

The ~ means update in place: plan will revert the change to match config. Use terraform plan -refresh-only -detailed-exitcode for drift reporting in CI: exit code 0 means no drift, 1 means error, 2 means drift detected — your pipeline can alert on 2 without proposing changes. Critical nuance for the panel: objects Terraform never managed (like a hand-created data disk with no resource block) are invisible to drift detection — plan cannot see what it does not track. Drift only covers managed resources; unmanaged objects must be imported first, which is exactly the data-disk scenario.
notes.title: Drift: when reality diverges from state

notes.body:
terraform import maps an existing real object to a resource block in your configuration and writes it into state — it never creates, modifies, or deletes cloud resources. The workflow is: write the resource block (it can start nearly empty), run terraform import <address> <provider-id>, run terraform plan, and reconcile any diff by filling in attributes until the plan is clean. Worked example: a storage account stlegacydata was created in the portal. You write:

resource "azurerm_storage_account" "legacy" {
  name                     = "stlegacydata"
  resource_group_name      = "rg-data"
  location                 = "eastus"
  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "LRS"
}

Then run terraform import azurerm_storage_account.legacy /subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/rg-data/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/stlegacydata. Import succeeds; terraform plan then shows which attributes your block got wrong (for example, it may propose changing access_tier because the real account differs). You adjust the block until plan is empty. Only then is the object truly under management. Classic import does not generate configuration — you write the block. Terraform 1.5+ also offers import blocks for config-driven bulk import, but the CLI flow above is the panel answer.
notes.title: terraform import: adopt, don't rebuild

notes.body:
The panel question: a data disk was added to a VM manually in Azure. It is not in the repo, it must be kept (data on it), and the team wants Terraform to manage it. The trap answers are 'delete it and let Terraform recreate it' (data loss) or 'leave it unmanaged' (drift blindness forever). The correct sequence, worked end to end. Step 1: write the resource block matching the real disk:

resource "azurerm_managed_disk" "app_data" {
  name                 = "vm-app-data-disk-01"
  location             = "eastus"
  resource_group_name  = "rg-app"
  storage_account_type = "Premium_LRS"
  create_option        = "Empty"
  disk_size_gb         = 128
}

Step 2: import it — terraform import azurerm_managed_disk.app_data /subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/rg-app/providers/Microsoft.Compute/disks/vm-app-data-disk-01. Step 3: also model the attachment with azurerm_virtual_machine_data_disk_attachment, importing it too (its ID is a composite of VM and disk IDs). Step 4: run terraform plan until it shows no changes, then commit. If plan still wants to replace the disk, your block does not match reality — fix the block, never apply a replacing plan onto a disk holding data. Say this sentence in the panel: 'Import is zero-downtime adoption; the plan must be empty before I commit, because a non-empty plan against a data disk is a data-loss risk.'
notes.title: Panel scenario: the manually added VM data disk

notes.body:
When a resource uses for_each, each instance's address includes its key in brackets: azurerm_managed_disk.data["logs"]. Your shell interprets brackets and quotes, so the address must be quoted as a single argument. The panel's exact command is: terraform import 'azurerm_managed_disk.example["disk1"]' <id> — single quotes around the whole address so the shell passes the double quotes through to Terraform untouched. Worked example: disks declared as

resource "azurerm_managed_disk" "data" {
  for_each = toset(["logs", "uploads"])
  name     = "vm-disk-${each.key}"
  ...
}

To import the logs disk: terraform import 'azurerm_managed_disk.data["logs"]' /subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/rg-app/providers/Microsoft.Compute/disks/vm-disk-logs. Without the quotes, bash treats ["logs"] as a glob pattern and the command fails with 'no matches found' or mangles the address. On Windows PowerShell the same single-quote wrapping works. Verify with terraform state list afterward — you should see azurerm_managed_disk.data["logs"] listed. Interview one-liner: 'Single-quote the full address; the shell must never see the brackets.'

mockTask.q: Panel: 'The dev team needs a storage account. They hand you three container names. Codify it in Terraform. (You whiteboard the for_each over toset.) Then: requirements changed — each container needs its own access type: private, blob, or container. How do you modify the code?'

notes.body: count creates N copies addressed by index: azurerm_storage_container.team[0], [1], [2]. for_each creates one instance per key: azurerm_storage_container.team["logs"]. The difference that matters is identity under change. Worked example: containers = ["logs", "reports", "uploads"] with count. Remove "reports" from the middle. Terraform now maps [0]=logs, [1]=uploads — the old [1] (reports) is destroyed and the old [2] (uploads) is destroyed and recreated as [1], because identity is positional. Two destroys and a recreate for a one-item removal, and the recreated container loses its blobs. With for_each over toset(["logs", "reports", "uploads"]), removing "reports" destroys only team["reports"]; logs and uploads are untouched because identity is the key. Interview rule: count for truly identical, fungible copies (three identical worker VMs); for_each whenever instances have names or individual settings — which is nearly always in real infrastructure.
notes.title: count vs for_each: index identity vs key identity

notes.body:
for_each accepts a map or a set of strings (use toset() to convert a list). Inside the block, each.key is the map key (or the set element), and each.value is the map value (or the same element for sets). Worked example — the panel scenario, phase 1. The dev team hands you container names; codify them:

resource "azurerm_storage_container" "team" {
  for_each              = toset(["logs", "reports", "uploads"])
  name                  = each.key
  storage_account_name  = azurerm_storage_account.data.name
  container_access_type = "private"
}

This creates team["logs"], team["reports"], team["uploads"], each named by its key. With a set, each.key and each.value are identical ("logs"), so use each.key for the name. The pattern to memorize: for_each = collection, name/address from each.key, per-instance settings from each.value. If you need different settings per instance, the collection must be a map — which is exactly what phase 2 of the scenario demands.

notes.body:
tfvars files assign values to variables: terraform.tfvars and *.auto.tfvars load automatically; anything else loads via -var-file. Worked example — environments/dev.tfvars:

account_name        = "stteamdatadev01"
environment         = "dev"
containers = {
  logs    = "private"
  reports = "blob"
}

environments/prod.tfvars:

account_name        = "stteamdataprod01"
environment         = "prod"
containers = {
  logs    = "private"
  reports = "private"
  uploads = "container"
}

Run with terraform plan -var-file=environments/prod.tfvars. The same module, two environments, zero code duplication — this is the enterprise pattern M35 builds on. Secrets rule: non-secret values may live in committed tfvars; anything secret goes in gitignored files (secrets.auto.tfvars in .gitignore) or environment variables (TF_VAR_db_password), never in the repo. Precedence to memorize: -var flags beat -var-file, which beats auto.tfvars, which beats defaults. Interview answer: 'tfvars separate what changes per environment from the code that stays identical.'

notes.body: Putting it together as you would in the panel whiteboard exercise. Layout: main.tf (provider + resource group), variables.tf, modules/storage/{main.tf,variables.tf,outputs.tf}, environments/{dev,prod}.tfvars. Step 1: terraform init — downloads the azurerm provider and registers the local module. Step 2: terraform fmt -recursive — canonical formatting; unformatted code fails CI lint gates. Step 3: terraform validate — checks syntax and type consistency without credentials; it catches a map(string) fed to a list(string) variable instantly. Step 4: terraform plan -var-file=environments/dev.tfvars -out=tfplan — review: 1 storage account + 2 containers to add, keys team["logs"] and team["reports"]. Step 5 (the phase-2 change): add uploads = "container" to dev.tfvars, re-plan — output shows exactly one addition, team["uploads"], and nothing else. That single-addition plan is the observable proof of key-based identity, and narrating it is what turns a code sample into a panel-winning answer.

notes.body: Four traps to memorize. Trap 1: for_each over a list — rejected; for_each needs a map or set of strings, so wrap lists in toset(). Trap 2: unknown keys at plan time — if the map comes from a resource attribute not known until apply (e.g., a computed ID), Terraform errors with 'for_each value depends on resource attributes'; the fix is deriving keys from variables or data known at plan time. Trap 3: mixing count and for_each in one block — forbidden; pick one. Trap 4: referencing instances — with for_each you cannot use splat-index syntax like team[*].name reliably for keyed lookup; use values(azurerm_storage_container.team)[*].name for lists or a for expression { for k, c in azurerm_storage_container.team : k => c.name } for maps. Worked example of the for expression producing a name-to-ID map for outputs: output "container_ids" { value = { for k, c in azurerm_storage_container.team : k => c.id } }. Interview line: 'for_each failures are almost always about keys not being known at plan time.'
notes.title: Common for_each traps and how to dodge them

notes.body:
The panel question 'walk me through Terraform from testing to prod' wants a promotion story, not a command list. Here is the shape: an engineer branches from main, writes or edits Terraform in a feature branch, and opens a pull request. CI runs terraform fmt -check, terraform validate, and terraform plan -var-file=environments/dev.tfvars, posting the plan as a PR comment. A reviewer approves; merge to main triggers apply to the dev environment automatically. Promotion is a second PR (or a release pipeline) that runs plan against stage with -var-file=environments/stage.tfvars; stage must be green — including QA's sign-off — before the same artifact (the same commit, the same saved plan file) is applied to prod, usually with a manual approval gate. Worked layout:

environments/{dev,stage,qa,prod}.tfvars
modules/...          # shared, versioned

No environment has its own copied code — only its own tfvars. The discipline the panel listens for: the exact plan file applied to prod was reviewed at the PR stage (terraform plan -out=tfplan, then terraform apply tfplan), so prod never applies a surprise.
notes.title: The enterprise lifecycle: testing to prod walkthrough

notes.body:
The panel's 'how was Terraform run at your previous job' answer starts here: secrets arrived as environment variables, never as committed files. Terraform natively reads any variable named TF_VAR_<name> as the value for variable <name>, and providers read their own (ARM_CLIENT_ID / ARM_CLIENT_SECRET / ARM_TENANT_ID / ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID for Azure; AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY for AWS). Worked example — a CI step:

export TF_VAR_db_password="$DB_PASSWORD"
export ARM_CLIENT_SECRET="$AZURE_SECRET"
terraform plan -var-file=environments/prod.tfvars -out=tfplan

The tfvars file holds non-secret per-environment values (names, SKUs, regions); the secrets ride in the process environment, which the CI system populates from its own secret store and masks in logs. Two rules: never echo secrets (even masked values can leak via set -x — use set +x around secret handling), and remember env vars still end up in the state file, so state storage lockdown from M33 remains mandatory. Interview line: 'Code on GitHub, secrets in env vars, tfvars for everything non-secret per environment.'
notes.title: Secrets via environment variables: the panel's answer

notes.body:
The corollary the panel explicitly named: tfvars carrying secrets are never committed. The pattern is a committed template plus an ignored real file. Worked example — commit secrets.tfvars.example:

db_password = "REPLACE_ME"
api_key     = "REPLACE_ME"

And .gitignore contains:

*.tfvars
!environments/*.tfvars
!secrets.tfvars.example

So environments/dev.tfvars (non-secret) is tracked, while any secrets-bearing tfvars is ignored. CI generates the secrets file at runtime from its vault or uses TF_VAR_ env vars instead. Verify locally with git check-ignore -v secrets.auto.tfvars — it should print the matching ignore rule. The failure mode this prevents is real: committed AWS keys get scraped by bots within minutes and the account gets cryptomined before lunch. Interview line: 'If a secret ever touches a committed file, we rotate it — no exceptions, no matter how fast we caught it.'

notes.body: Two ways to run one codebase against multiple environments. Workspaces: terraform workspace new dev creates a separate state (same backend, key prefixed with env:) while the code and variables stay identical — you switch with terraform workspace select prod and re-apply. Directories: environments/dev/main.tf (or one root with per-env tfvars, as in this module) keeps entirely separate state files and working directories. Worked comparison: workspaces are cheap and built in — terraform workspace list shows dev, stage, prod — but every workspace shares one backend configuration, so a backend outage or a mis-targeted select can hit the wrong environment, and secrets handling is identical across them. Directories (or separate tfvars per env with separate pipeline jobs) give blast-radius isolation: prod's state, credentials scope, and approvals are fully separate artifacts. The enterprise answer: directories (or distinct pipeline stages with their own state keys) for prod separation; workspaces for cheap personal/branch sandboxes. Interview line: 'Workspaces for experiments, directories for environments — prod deserves its own state, its own credentials, and its own gate.'

notes.body:
An Ansible playbook is YAML: a list of plays, each play targeting hosts and running a list of tasks. Tasks call modules (apt, copy, service, template) with arguments. Ansible is idempotent by design — running the same playbook twice changes nothing the second time, because modules check state before acting. Worked example — site.yml:

---
- name: Configure web servers
  hosts: webservers
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: Install nginx
      ansible.builtin.apt:
        name: nginx
        state: present
        update_cache: true

    - name: Ensure nginx is running
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: started
        enabled: true

Run with ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml. Run it again: both tasks report ok (no change) instead of changed — that ok-on-rerun is idempotency, and the panel will ask you to demonstrate or explain it. Contrast with a raw shell script, which would reinstall and restart blindly every run. Interview line: 'Tasks describe desired state per resource; modules make reruns safe.'
notes.title: Playbooks, plays, tasks: the anatomy

notes.body:
Handlers are tasks that run only when notified by a changed task, and they run once at the end of the play even if notified multiple times. The classic use is restarting a service after its config changes. Worked example:

  tasks:
    - name: Deploy nginx config
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: nginx.conf.j2
        dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
        mode: "0644"
      notify: Restart nginx

  handlers:
    - name: Restart nginx
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: restarted

First run: template changes the file (changed) -> handler fires -> nginx restarts. Second run: file already matches (ok) -> no notify -> handler skipped. Predict-the-output drill: if three tasks all notify 'Restart nginx' and all three change, the handler still runs exactly once. Handlers also support listen for grouping (multiple handlers listening on one topic). Interview line: 'notify plus handlers is how Ansible avoids restarting services on every run — restarts happen only when config actually changed.'
notes.title: Handlers: react only when notified

notes.body:
Variables come from playbooks (vars:), inventory, group_vars/, or facts. Templates render Jinja2 (.j2) files with those variables. register — the panel's explicit question — captures a task's result into a variable for later tasks. Worked example:

  tasks:
    - name: Check free disk space
      ansible.builtin.command: df -h /var | tail -1
      register: disk_out
      changed_when: false

    - name: Show disk usage
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "VAR partition: {{ disk_out.stdout }}"

    - name: Fail if disk is over 90 percent full
      ansible.builtin.fail:
        msg: "Disk critically full: {{ disk_out.stdout }}"
      when: "'90%' in disk_out.stdout or '91%' in disk_out.stdout"

register stores stdout, stderr, rc, changed, and more; changed_when: false marks read-only commands so they report ok instead of changed (keeping reruns clean). when: gates tasks on the captured data. Interview answer to 'how do you capture command output': 'register the task into a variable, then use .stdout / .stdout_lines / .rc in debug, when, or fail — with changed_when: false on read-only commands.'
notes.title: Variables, templates, and register: capturing output

notes.body:
A role is a directory with a conventional layout — tasks/, handlers/, templates/, files/, vars/, defaults/, meta/ — that turns a playbook's logic into a shareable unit. Create one with ansible-galaxy init webserver; the layout appears with main.yml entry points in each directory. Worked example — roles/webserver/tasks/main.yml:

---
- name: Install nginx
  ansible.builtin.apt:
    name: nginx
    state: present
  notify: Restart nginx

and roles/webserver/handlers/main.yml holds the restart handler. Consume it from a playbook:

---
- name: Configure web tier
  hosts: webservers
  become: true
  roles:
    - webserver

Role variables layer cleanly: defaults/ (lowest priority, overridable) vs vars/ (higher). Galaxy (galaxy.ansible.com) hosts community roles, but enterprises usually vendor their own. Interview line: 'Roles are Ansible's modules from M34 — the reuse unit. Playbooks compose roles; roles compose tasks.' The panel's 'most interesting role' question is really asking whether you have built one — after this module's lab, you have.
notes.title: Roles: packaging automation for reuse

notes.body:
Inventory maps hostnames to groups; playbooks target groups, never individual machines by habit. INI and YAML formats both work, and groups nest via :children. Worked example - inventory.ini:

[webservers]
web01.example.com
web02.example.com

[dbservers]
db01.example.com

[prod:children]
webservers
dbservers

Variables attach per host or per group: a host line can carry ansible_user=deployer ansible_host=10.0.0.5, and a [webservers:vars] section sets values for the whole group. Host variables beat group variables beat play variables in the precedence chain - worth memorizing for debugging 'why did my variable not apply' questions. Ad-hoc commands skip playbooks for one-offs: ansible webservers -i inventory.ini -m ping checks connectivity, and ansible webservers -i inventory.ini -m ansible.builtin.apt -a 'name=htop state=present' --become installs a package across the tier in one line. At scale, static files go stale, so dynamic inventory (a plugin or script returning host JSON) queries Azure or AWS at run time - inventory always reflects reality. Interview line: 'Static inventory for the lab, dynamic inventory for the cloud - either way, groups are how one playbook addresses a whole tier.'
notes.title: Inventory: who Ansible talks to

notes.body: Ansible has cloud modules (azure_rm_virtualmachine and friends) that can create VMs, so the panel's challenge is fair — and the answer is about models, not features. Terraform is declarative with state: it records what it created, detects drift on every plan, and converges reality to config — including deleting what should not exist. Ansible is procedural without state: a playbook that creates a VM will happily create a second one on rerun unless you write careful idempotency guards, it cannot show you a plan of what will change, and it cannot detect that someone resized the VM in the portal. Worked contrast: delete the VM in the portal. Terraform: next plan shows '1 to add' — it knows. Ansible: rerunning the playbook recreates it only if your tasks check existence first; nothing ever reports the deletion. The enterprise answer: Terraform provisions the platform (the relatively static, expensive, stateful layer — VNets, VMs, storage), Ansible configures inside it (packages, files, services — the fast-changing layer). Use each for its strength; the panel wants that sentence, not a tool war.

Panel deep-dive 2: removing resources — Terraform vs Ansible

notes.body: Memorize this matrix; the panel's 'biggest difference' question is answered by the first row. | Dimension | Terraform | Ansible | |---|---|---| | Model | Declarative desired state + state file | Procedural tasks, no state | | Change preview | terraform plan (reviewable diff) | --check mode (best effort, not a true plan) | | Drift detection | Built in — refresh on every plan | None — reruns only converge what tasks cover | | Removal | Config deletion + apply = planned destroy | state: absent task you authored, no preview | | Language | HCL | YAML playbooks | | Agent | Agentless (provider APIs) | Agentless (SSH/WinRM) | | Sweet spot | Provisioning: networks, VMs, storage, DNS | Configuration: packages, files, services, app deploys | | Multi-cloud | One workflow, provider plugins | Cloud modules exist but config mgmt is the strength | | Secrets | Via Vault provider / env (M35) | Ansible Vault (encrypted vars/files) |. The synthesis the panel rewards: they are complements, not competitors — Terraform builds the datacenter, Ansible configures the servers inside it, and Jenkins (M38) orchestrates both. Say: 'I provision with Terraform, configure with Ansible, and I can tell you exactly where each one's job ends.'
